title: Comparing exam performances by z-score
stem: Priya scored 83 on a chemistry exam whose scores have mean 74 and standard deviation 6. Marcus scored 68 on a history exam whose scores have mean 61 and standard deviation 4. Which student performed better relative to the other students who took the same exam?

correct.text: Marcus, because his z-score of 1.75 is higher than Priya's z-score of 1.5.
correct.rationale: Priya's z = (83 - 74)/6 = 1.5. Marcus's z = (68 - 61)/4 = 1.75. Standardizing puts the two exams on a common scale, and Marcus is farther above his own mean in standard-deviation units.

wrong.text: Priya, because her raw score of 83 is higher than Marcus's raw score of 68.
wrong.rationale: The exams have different means and standard deviations, so raw scores cannot be compared directly; 83 corresponds to z = 1.5 while 68 corresponds to z = 1.75.

wrong.text: Priya, because she is 9 points above her mean while Marcus is only 7 points above his.
wrong.rationale: Raw distances from the mean ignore the spread of each exam. Priya's 9 points is 9/6 = 1.5 SDs, while Marcus's 7 points is 7/4 = 1.75 SDs.
wrong.error_pattern: compares raw distance from the mean ignoring SD

wrong.text: Priya, because her score is about 1.12 times her exam's mean, compared with about 1.11 times for Marcus.
wrong.rationale: Dividing a score by its mean is not standardizing: 83/74 is about 1.12 and 68/61 is about 1.11, but this ignores the SDs. Using z-scores, Marcus (1.75) beats Priya (1.5).
wrong.error_pattern: divides by mean instead of standardizing

change_note: New context, different numbers; correct answer flips from the seed (lower raw score wins); distractors include a ratio-to-mean error.

title: Salary relative to company pay distributions
stem: Lena earns $52,000 at a firm where salaries have mean $45,000 and standard deviation $4,000. Omar earns $61,000 at a different firm where salaries have mean $50,000 and standard deviation $7,000. Relative to the pay at their own firms, who is paid better?

correct.text: Lena, because her z-score of 1.75 exceeds Omar's z-score of about 1.57.
correct.rationale: Lena's z = (52,000 - 45,000)/4,000 = 1.75. Omar's z = (61,000 - 50,000)/7,000 = about 1.57. Lena sits farther above her firm's mean in standard-deviation units.

wrong.text: Omar, because $61,000 is a larger salary than $52,000.
wrong.rationale: The firms have different pay distributions, so raw salaries are not comparable. Standardizing gives z = 1.75 for Lena and about 1.57 for Omar.

wrong.text: Omar, because he earns $11,000 above his firm's mean while Lena earns only $7,000 above hers.
wrong.rationale: Dollar distances from the mean ignore each firm's spread. $7,000 is 1.75 SDs of Lena's firm; $11,000 is only about 1.57 SDs of Omar's firm.
wrong.error_pattern: compares raw distance from the mean

wrong.text: Omar, because his salary is 22% above his firm's mean while Lena's is only 16% above hers.
wrong.rationale: Percent above the mean (11,000/50,000 = 22% and 7,000/45,000 = about 16%) is not a standardized comparison because it ignores SDs. Using z-scores, Lena (1.75) is higher than Omar (about 1.57).
wrong.error_pattern: uses percent of mean instead of SD units

change_note: Different domain (salaries) and numbers; distractor set targets percent-of-mean confusion; z-scores are close but distinct.

title: Which result is more unusual
stem: Tom scored 35 on a placement test with mean 50 and standard deviation 10. Sue scored 58 on a different placement test with mean 50 and standard deviation 4. Whose result is farther from the typical score on her or his own test, measured in standard deviations?

correct.text: Sue's, because her z-score of 2.0 is larger in absolute value than Tom's z-score of -1.5.
correct.rationale: Tom's z = (35 - 50)/10 = -1.5, so he is 1.5 SDs below the mean. Sue's z = (58 - 50)/4 = 2.0, so she is 2.0 SDs above the mean. Distance from the mean in SD units is the absolute z-score, and 2.0 > 1.5.

wrong.text: Tom's, because 35 is lower than 58.
wrong.rationale: Which raw score is lower does not determine distance from the mean in SD units; Tom is 1.5 SDs from his mean and Sue is 2.0 SDs from hers.

wrong.text: Tom's, because he is 15 points from his mean while Sue is only 8 points from hers.
wrong.rationale: Raw point distances ignore the spreads. Tom's 15 points is 1.5 SDs while Sue's 8 points is 2.0 SDs.

wrong.text: Neither, because Tom's negative z-score of -1.5 shows he performed worse than Sue and the two cannot be compared.
wrong.rationale: A z-score of -1.5 and one of 2.0 can be compared by magnitude: the question asks for distance from the mean, which is |z|. |-1.5| = 1.5 is smaller than |2.0| = 2.0.

change_note: Asks for distance from the mean (absolute z) with one negative z, a new twist on the same standardizing skill.

title: Quadrupling n for a skewed waiting-time mean
stem: Waiting times at a walk-in clinic are strongly right-skewed with standard deviation 12 minutes. A researcher repeatedly takes simple random samples of patients and computes the sample mean waiting time. Compare the sampling distribution of the sample mean for n = 20 patients with that for n = 80 patients.

correct.text: The shape is closer to normal for n = 80, and the standard error is cut in half, from about 2.7 to about 1.3 minutes.
correct.rationale: By the Central Limit Theorem the sampling distribution of x-bar is closer to normal for the larger sample. SE = 12/sqrt(20) is about 2.68 and 12/sqrt(80) is about 1.34, so quadrupling n halves the SE.

wrong.text: The shape is closer to normal for n = 80, and the standard error is cut to one-fourth, from about 2.7 to about 0.7 minutes.
wrong.rationale: The shape part is right, but SE shrinks with the square root of n, not n: 12/sqrt(80) is about 1.34, not 2.68/4 = 0.67.

wrong.text: The shape is still right-skewed like the population for both sizes, and the standard error is cut in half from about 2.7 to about 1.3 minutes.
wrong.rationale: The SE values are right but the shape claim is not: as n grows, the sampling distribution of x-bar becomes more nearly normal even though the population is skewed.

wrong.text: The shape is closer to normal for n = 80, but the standard error stays at 12 minutes for both sample sizes.
wrong.rationale: The standard error of x-bar is sigma/sqrt(n), not sigma; it is about 2.68 minutes for n = 20 and 1.34 minutes for n = 80.

change_note: Quantified version with a clinic context; includes specific SE values (12/sqrt(n)).

title: Quadrupling the sample size and the SE
stem: A hospital studies lengths of stay, which are right-skewed with standard deviation 6 days. The mean stay in a random sample of 36 patients is compared with the mean stay in a random sample of 144 patients. How do the standard errors of the two sample means compare?

correct.text: The sample of 144 has half the standard error of the sample of 36: 0.5 days versus 1.0 days.
correct.rationale: SE = 6/sqrt(36) = 1.0 day and SE = 6/sqrt(144) = 0.5 day. Four times as many patients cuts the standard error by a factor of sqrt(4) = 2.

wrong.text: The sample of 144 has one-fourth the standard error of the sample of 36: 0.25 days versus 1.0 days.
wrong.rationale: SE falls with the square root of the sample size, so quadrupling n halves the SE. 6/sqrt(144) = 0.5, not 0.25.

wrong.text: The two samples have the same standard error of 6 days, since both come from the same population.
wrong.rationale: The SE of x-bar is sigma/sqrt(n) and depends on n: it is 1.0 day for n = 36 and 0.5 day for n = 144, not the population SD of 6.

wrong.text: The sample of 144 has twice the standard error of the sample of 36, because more patients add more variation.
wrong.rationale: More observations do not add variability to the mean; averaging more values makes x-bar more stable. SE is 0.5 day at n = 144 and 1.0 day at n = 36.

change_note: Focus on quantitative effect of n on SE for a skewed population rather than shape; new context and numbers.

title: Sampling distribution of mean daily rainfall
stem: Daily rainfall in a region is strongly right-skewed, with mean 3 mm and standard deviation 4 mm. Random samples of 64 days are taken and the sample mean rainfall is computed for each. Which description of the sampling distribution of the sample mean is best?

correct.text: Approximately normal, with mean 3 mm and standard error 0.5 mm.
correct.rationale: The mean of x-bar equals the population mean, 3 mm. SE = 4/sqrt(64) = 0.5 mm. With n = 64 the Central Limit Theorem makes the shape approximately normal.

wrong.text: Right-skewed like the population, with mean 3 mm and standard error 0.5 mm.
wrong.rationale: The center and spread are right, but with n = 64 the CLT makes the sampling distribution of x-bar approximately normal rather than skewed like the population.

wrong.text: Approximately normal, with mean 3 mm and standard error 4 mm.
wrong.rationale: The shape and center are right, but SE = 4/sqrt(64) = 0.5 mm; 4 mm is the spread of individual days, not of sample means.

wrong.text: Approximately normal, with mean 0.375 mm and standard error 0.5 mm.
wrong.rationale: The mean of the sampling distribution is the population mean, 3 mm, not 3/8. Only the spread is divided by sqrt(n) (4/8 = 0.5).

change_note: Asks for the full description (shape, center, spread) with computed values.

title: z-score of a plant below the mean
stem: The heights of seedlings in a greenhouse have mean 35 cm and standard deviation 4 cm. What is the z-score of a seedling that is 29 cm tall?

correct.rationale: z = (29 - 35)/4 = -6/4 = -1.5; the seedling is 1.5 SDs below the mean.

wrong.rationale: The magnitude is right but the sign is wrong: 29 is below the mean of 35, so the z-score must be negative.
This is only the raw difference 29 - 35; it was not divided by the standard deviation of 4.
This divides the difference by the mean (-6/35, about -0.17) instead of by the standard deviation 4.

change_note: New context; below-mean value; distractors target missing division, sign, and dividing by the mean.

title: z-score of a delivery time
stem: Package delivery times for a courier have mean 64 minutes and standard deviation 5 minutes. A particular delivery took 72 minutes. What is its z-score?

wrong.rationale: This is the raw difference 72 - 64; it was never divided by the standard deviation 5.
This is 72/64, a ratio of the value to the mean, rather than (72 - 64)/5.
This is 72/5: the value was divided by the SD without first subtracting the mean 64.

change_note: New context and numbers; error patterns differ from seed.

title: z-score of a fast run
stem: The time for a school's students to finish a puzzle has mean 12.5 minutes and standard deviation 2.5 minutes. A student finishes in 10 minutes. Find the z-score for this student.

wrong.rationale: The size is correct but the student finished faster than the mean, so the z-score must be negative.
This is only the difference 10 - 12.5; it was not divided by the SD of 2.5.
This is 10/2.5: the value was divided by the SD without subtracting the mean first.

change_note: Different context; value below mean with decimal numbers.

title: Median of six ordered values
stem: Six commute times (in minutes), listed in order, are 3, 5, 7, 8, 12, 15. What is the median commute time?

correct.rationale: With n = 6 the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th values: (7 + 8)/2 = 7.5.

wrong.rationale: This is the mean of all six values (50/6, about 8.3), not the median.
This adds the two middle values (7 + 8 = 15) without dividing by 2.
wrong.error_pattern: adds middle values instead of averaging

wrong.rationale: This takes only the 3rd value; with an even number of values, the median must average the two middle ones.

change_note: Explicit data list with an outlier-ish value so mean differs from median.

title: Median position for 30 ordered values
stem: A researcher has 30 test scores arranged from smallest to largest. Which description locates the median of these scores?

correct.text: The mean of the 15th and 16th ordered scores.
correct.rationale: With 30 values, the two middle positions are 15 and 16, and the median is their average.

wrong.text: The 15th ordered score alone.
wrong.rationale: Using only the 15th value would be right only if the count were odd; with 30 values the median averages the 15th and 16th.

wrong.text: The 16th ordered score alone, since 30/2 + 1 = 16.
wrong.rationale: The position (n + 1)/2 = 15.5 falls halfway between the 15th and 16th values, so both must be averaged.

wrong.text: The mean of the 1st and 30th ordered scores.
wrong.rationale: This is the midrange (average of min and max), which is not the median.

change_note: Conceptual positions for n = 30 instead of 20.

title: Median of twelve ordered values
stem: The monthly rainfall totals (mm) for a city, sorted from least to greatest, are 4, 6, 6, 9, 10, 12, 13, 15, 18, 21, 25, 40. What is the median?

correct.rationale: With n = 12 the middle values are the 6th (12) and 7th (13), so the median is (12 + 13)/2 = 12.5.

wrong.rationale: This is only the 6th value; with 12 values the median averages the 6th and 7th.
This is the mean of all 12 values (179/12, about 14.9), pulled up by the value 40; it is not the median.
This is the average of the positions 6 and 7, not of the values stored at those positions.

change_note: Longer list, skewed so mean and median differ.

title: Simple random sample from a registry
stem: A city council wants a simple random sample of 40 residents from a registry listing 2,000 residents. Which procedure best accomplishes this?

correct.text: Number the residents 1 to 2,000 and use a random number generator to draw 40 different numbers.
correct.rationale: Numbering every resident and drawing distinct random numbers gives each resident, and each group of 40, the same chance of selection, which defines a simple random sample.

wrong.text: Interview the first 40 people who walk into city hall on Monday morning.
wrong.rationale: This is a convenience sample: people at city hall on a Monday are not randomly chosen and are unlikely to represent all residents.

wrong.text: Mail a survey to all residents and use the first 40 that are returned.
wrong.rationale: Those who respond first are self-selected, so this is a voluntary response sample that is prone to bias.

wrong.text: Take the first 40 residents on the registry, which is sorted by last name.
wrong.rationale: The first 40 names alphabetically are a fixed group, not randomly chosen; most residents have no chance of selection.

change_note: City registry context; distractors cover convenience, voluntary response and fixed-block selection.

title: Random sample of gym members
stem: A gym has 250 members and wants feedback from a simple random sample of 25 of them. Which plan is best?

correct.text: Give each member an ID from 1 to 250 and have software pick 25 different IDs at random.
correct.rationale: Random selection from a complete numbered list gives every member and every group of 25 the same chance of being chosen, which is the definition of an SRS.

wrong.text: Survey the 25 members who visit the gym most often.
wrong.rationale: Frequent visitors differ systematically from other members, so this non-random choice builds in bias.

wrong.text: Post a sign inviting members to take a survey and use the first 25 who respond.
wrong.rationale: Members who volunteer are self-selected, which creates voluntary response bias rather than a random sample.

wrong.text: Ask the 25 members who are nearest the front desk at noon on Tuesday.
wrong.rationale: Whoever is convenient at one time and place is a convenience sample; most members have no chance of being chosen.

change_note: Gym context; different distractor wording and numbers.

title: Random sample of seniors
stem: A principal wants a simple random sample of 50 seniors from the 400 students in the senior class. Which method should she use?

correct.text: Number the seniors 1 to 400 and use a random number generator for 50 distinct numbers.
correct.rationale: Each senior is equally likely to be chosen, and every set of 50 seniors is equally likely, so this is a simple random sample.

wrong.text: Select the 50 seniors who have the highest grade point averages.
wrong.rationale: Choosing by GPA is a deliberate, non-random rule that excludes lower-GPA students and biases the sample.

wrong.text: Ask each of the 10 homeroom teachers to hand-pick the 5 students they prefer.
wrong.rationale: Teachers choose by their own judgment, so students are not selected by chance and bias is likely.

wrong.text: Announce a pizza party and take the first 50 seniors who sign up for it.
wrong.rationale: Students who sign up are self-selected, so this voluntary response sample is not random.

change_note: Different population size; incentive-based voluntary response distractor.

title: Confounder for ice cream and drownings
stem: Public health data show that in months when ice cream sales are higher, more drownings occur. Which of the following is a plausible confounding variable for this association?

correct.text: Hot weather, which draws more people to swim and also increases ice cream purchases
correct.rationale: A confounder is linked to both variables. Warm weather leads to more swimming (more drownings) and to more ice cream sales, which can produce the association without either causing the other.

wrong.text: The number of drownings reported in each month
wrong.rationale: This is the response variable itself, not a third variable that influences both quantities.

wrong.text: The correlation between the monthly ice cream sales and drownings
wrong.rationale: The correlation is a summary of the association, not a separate variable acting on both measurements.
wrong.error_pattern: confuses a summary statistic with a confounder

wrong.text: The year in which the data were recorded, with no link to either quantity
wrong.rationale: A variable with no relationship to swimming or to ice cream sales cannot create the association, so it cannot be a confounder.

change_note: Classic confounding scenario from a different domain; distractors tied to variable-role errors.

title: Confounder for piano lessons and math scores
stem: A school district finds that students who take piano lessons score higher on math tests than students who do not. Which is a plausible confounding variable?

correct.text: Family income, which could affect both lesson enrollment and math scores
correct.rationale: A third variable that influences both who takes lessons and how students do in math can create the observed association with no causal effect of lessons.

wrong.text: The average math score earned by the group of students taking lessons
wrong.rationale: This is a summary of the response variable for one group, not a separate variable influencing both lessons and scores.
wrong.error_pattern: confuses a group statistic with a confounder

wrong.text: The p-value from comparing the math scores of the two groups
wrong.rationale: The p-value summarizes evidence from the data; it does not affect who takes lessons or how well students do.
wrong.error_pattern: confuses test output with a confounder

wrong.text: The total number of students included in the district study
wrong.rationale: Sample size affects precision of estimates, but it does not influence both lesson-taking and math scores for individual students.
wrong.error_pattern: confuses sample size with a confounder

change_note: Education context; confounder is a socio-economic third variable.

title: Confounder for fitness trackers and BMI
stem: An observational study finds that adults who wear fitness trackers have lower body mass index (BMI), on average, than adults who do not. Which is a plausible confounding variable?

correct.text: Health consciousness, causing people to wear trackers and keep a lower BMI
correct.rationale: A trait that affects both tracker use and BMI could explain the association even if trackers have no effect on BMI.

wrong.text: The BMI values that were measured for the adults in the study
wrong.rationale: BMI is the response variable being compared, not a third variable influencing both groups' tracker use and outcome.

wrong.text: The number of adults who were included in the study sample group
wrong.rationale: Sample size influences precision, but it does not drive both tracker use and BMI.
wrong.error_pattern: confuses sample size with a confounder

wrong.text: The test statistic used to compare BMI between the two groups
wrong.rationale: A test statistic summarizes the data after collection and cannot influence who wears a tracker or their BMI.
wrong.error_pattern: confuses test statistic with a confounder

change_note: Fitness context; same skill with new variables.

title: Inspecting every restaurant
stem: A city health department inspects every one of the 312 restaurants in the city. Which term best describes the way these data were collected?

correct.text: A census, because every restaurant in the population was included
correct.rationale: A census collects data from every member of the population of interest; here all 312 restaurants were inspected.

wrong.text: A cluster sample, because restaurants are grouped by neighborhood
wrong.rationale: A cluster sample includes only some selected clusters; here every restaurant was inspected, so nothing was sampled.

wrong.text: A systematic sample, because inspectors go through restaurants in street-address order
wrong.rationale: A systematic sample takes every kth unit; here all units are taken, so it is a census, not a sample.

wrong.text: A convenience sample, because easy-to-reach restaurants were inspected
wrong.rationale: A convenience sample takes only readily available units; here all restaurants were inspected, not only the easy ones.

change_note: Restaurant inspection context; distractors name other sampling types.

title: Employee satisfaction survey
stem: A company with 1,200 employees emails its satisfaction survey to every employee. What is the best name for this data collection method?

correct.text: A census of the company's employees
correct.rationale: Every employee in the population of interest was asked to participate, so it is a census, even though some may not respond.

wrong.text: A voluntary response sample
wrong.rationale: In a voluntary response sample, people choose whether to be included by responding to an open invitation; here the company contacts every employee, so there is no sampling.

wrong.text: A stratified random sample by department
wrong.rationale: Stratified sampling selects some units from each stratum; here all employees are contacted.

wrong.text: A simple random sample of 1,200 employees
wrong.rationale: The company has only 1,200 employees, so choosing 1,200 of them is not a random draw but everyone.

change_note: Workplace context; distractors include voluntary response.

title: Weighing every giraffe
stem: A zoo veterinarian weighs all 15 giraffes at the zoo to describe the herd. What is this called?

correct.text: A census of the herd
correct.rationale: All 15 giraffes in the population of interest were measured, so no sampling was involved.

wrong.text: A random sample of giraffes
wrong.rationale: A random sample uses chance to pick only some members of the population; here all 15 were measured.

wrong.text: A convenience sample
wrong.rationale: A convenience sample would include only easy-to-reach animals; here every giraffe was weighed.

wrong.text: An experiment
wrong.rationale: An experiment imposes treatments on subjects; simply weighing animals imposes none, so it is an observational census.

change_note: Zoo context; adds experiment-vs-census confusion.

title: Expected winnings on a prize wheel
stem: At a school carnival, a prize wheel pays $20 with probability 0.15, $5 with probability 0.30, and $0 otherwise. What are a player's expected winnings per spin?

wrong.rationale: This is the unweighted mean of the three payouts, (20 + 5 + 0)/3, which ignores their probabilities.
This counts only the $20 prize (20 x 0.15) and leaves out the $5 prize's contribution of $1.50.
This multiplies the largest prize by the total probability of any win: 20 x 0.45 = 9, overstating the value of the $5 prize.
wrong.error_pattern: applies total win probability to the top prize

change_note: Three-outcome game; distractors target unweighted mean and omission.

title: Mean of a discrete random variable
stem: The number of pets X owned by a randomly chosen student has this distribution: P(X = 0) = 0.1, P(X = 1) = 0.4, P(X = 2) = 0.3, P(X = 3) = 0.2. What is the expected value of X?

wrong.rationale: This is the unweighted mean of the values 0, 1, 2, 3, which ignores the probabilities.
This is the average of the four probabilities (1/4), not a probability-weighted average of the values.
This is the most likely value (mode), not the probability-weighted mean of the distribution.

change_note: Table-style discrete distribution instead of a two-outcome game.

title: Insurer's expected profit per policy
stem: An insurance company sells a policy for $60. With probability 0.02 it pays a claim of $2,000, and otherwise it pays nothing. What is the company's expected profit per policy, after the claim cost but including the $60 premium?

correct.rationale: Expected claim cost = 2,000(0.02) = $40, so expected profit = 60 - 40 = $20.

wrong.rationale: This is the expected claim payout only; the $60 premium was not subtracted from it.
The sign is reversed: expected profit is premium minus expected claim cost, 60 - 40 = +20, not 40 - 60.
This is only the premium; the expected payout of $40 per policy was not subtracted.

change_note: Net-profit framing with premium and claim; slightly harder than seed.

title: Comparing SE for two sample sizes
stem: A population has standard deviation 14. Researchers take one random sample of 49 observations and another of 196 observations and compute each sample mean. Which sample mean has the smaller standard error, and what are the two standard errors?

correct.text: The sample of 196, with standard errors of 2.0 for n = 49 and 1.0 for n = 196
correct.rationale: SE = 14/sqrt(49) = 2.0 and SE = 14/sqrt(196) = 1.0, so the larger sample has the smaller standard error.

wrong.text: The sample of 49, with standard errors of 1.0 for n = 49 and 2.0 for n = 196
wrong.rationale: This reverses the effect of sample size: SE is 14/7 = 2.0 for n = 49 and 14/14 = 1.0 for n = 196.

wrong.text: The sample of 196, with standard errors of 0.29 for n = 49 and 0.07 for n = 196
wrong.rationale: This divides 14 by n instead of the square root of n (14/49, 14/196). The correct SEs are 2.0 and 1.0.

wrong.text: Neither; both have a standard error of 14 because they come from the same population
wrong.rationale: The SE of the sample mean is sigma/sqrt(n), so it depends on n; it equals 14 only for n = 1.

change_note: Quantified comparison with given sigma.

title: Sample size needed to halve SE
stem: A random sample of n = 30 is used to estimate a population mean. By what sample size would the standard error of the sample mean be exactly half as large?

correct.rationale: SE is proportional to 1/sqrt(n). Halving SE needs sqrt(n) to double, so n must quadruple: 4 x 30 = 120.

wrong.rationale: Doubling n shrinks SE only by a factor of 1/sqrt(2), to about 71% of the original, not to half.
Cutting n in half makes SE larger, by a factor of sqrt(2), not smaller.
wrong.error_pattern: moves n in the wrong direction

wrong.rationale: Tripling n shrinks SE by a factor of 1/sqrt(3), to about 58% of the original, not to half.

change_note: Asks for sample size to halve SE; requires sqrt(n) reasoning.

title: SE of a sample mean commute time
stem: Commute times in a district have standard deviation 10 minutes. A simple random sample of 25 students is taken. What is the standard error of the sample mean commute time?

correct.text: 2.0 minutes
correct.rationale: SE = sigma/sqrt(n) = 10/sqrt(25) = 10/5 = 2.0.

wrong.text: 10 minutes
wrong.rationale: This is the standard deviation of individual commute times, not the standard error of the mean of 25 of them.

wrong.text: 0.4 minutes
wrong.rationale: This divides sigma by n (10/25) rather than by sqrt(n) = 5.

wrong.text: 50 minutes
wrong.rationale: This multiplies sigma by sqrt(n) (10 x 5) instead of dividing; SE should be smaller than sigma, not larger.

change_note: Direct calculation instead of qualitative comparison.

title: Decision with a strict alpha
stem: A test of whether a tutoring program raises mean scores gives a p-value of 0.032. The significance level chosen before the study was alpha = 0.01. What is the appropriate decision?

correct.text: Fail to reject H0, because 0.032 is greater than 0.01
correct.rationale: The p-value exceeds the chosen alpha, so the data do not provide convincing evidence against the null hypothesis at the 0.01 level.

wrong.text: Reject H0, because 0.032 is below the conventional 0.05 cutoff
wrong.rationale: The decision must use the alpha chosen for the study, 0.01. Since 0.032 > 0.01, the result is not significant.
wrong.error_pattern: uses default 0.05 instead of stated alpha

wrong.text: Reject H0, because the p-value is greater than alpha, showing a significant result
wrong.rationale: The inequality is reversed: significance requires p-value < alpha, and here 0.032 > 0.01.

wrong.text: Fail to reject H0 and conclude the tutoring program has no effect
wrong.rationale: Failing to reject H0 does not prove the program has no effect; it only means the evidence was not strong enough at alpha = 0.01.
wrong.error_pattern: treats failure to reject as proof of H0

change_note: Fail-to-reject case with stricter alpha; includes use-0.05-instead-of-alpha trap.

title: Decision and conclusion in context
stem: A company tests H0: mu = 10 hours against Ha: mu is not 10 hours for the mean battery life of a new phone. The test gives a p-value of 0.003, and alpha = 0.05. Which conclusion is correct?

correct.text: Reject H0; there is convincing evidence the mean battery life differs from 10 hours.
correct.rationale: Since 0.003 < 0.05, the data are unlikely under H0, so we reject it and conclude the mean differs from 10 hours.

wrong.text: Fail to reject H0, because the p-value of 0.003 is smaller than alpha
wrong.rationale: The rule is reversed: a p-value smaller than alpha leads to rejecting H0, not failing to reject.

wrong.text: Reject H0, because there is only a 0.3% chance that H0 is true
wrong.rationale: The p-value is the probability of results this extreme if H0 is true, not the probability that H0 is true.

wrong.text: Reject H0, which proves the true mean is not exactly 10 hours
wrong.rationale: Rejecting H0 is statistical evidence, not proof; a significance test cannot establish a conclusion with certainty.

change_note: Two-sided test with conclusion in context; p-value misinterpretation distractor.

title: Decision at alpha = 0.10
stem: A one-sample test of a population mean results in a p-value of 0.07. The researcher specified alpha = 0.10 before collecting data. What decision should be made?

correct.text: Reject H0, because 0.07 is less than 0.10
correct.rationale: The p-value is below the stated significance level of 0.10, so there is statistically significant evidence against H0.

wrong.text: Fail to reject H0, because 0.07 is greater than the usual 0.05 cutoff
wrong.rationale: The cutoff is the alpha stated for this study, 0.10, not 0.05; since 0.07 < 0.10 the result is significant.
wrong.error_pattern: uses default 0.05 instead of stated alpha

wrong.text: Reject H0 and conclude the probability H0 is true is 7%
wrong.rationale: The p-value is the probability of data this extreme assuming H0 is true, not the probability that H0 is true.

wrong.text: Make no decision until the test statistic is converted to a z-score
wrong.rationale: The p-value can be compared directly with alpha; no further conversion is needed to decide.
wrong.error_pattern: thinks p cannot be compared directly

change_note: Rejection case at alpha = 0.10; avoids default-0.05 reasoning.

title: Expected count from marginal totals
stem: In a chi-square test of independence, one cell of the table has row total 60, column total 90, and the table total is 300. What is the expected count for that cell?

correct.rationale: Expected count = (row total x column total)/table total = (60 x 90)/300 = 5400/300 = 18.

wrong.rationale: This divides by 150, half of the table total, instead of 300: (60 x 90)/150 = 36.
This adds the row and column totals (60 + 90) instead of multiplying them and dividing by the table total.
This multiplies the row and column totals (60 x 90) but never divides by the table total of 300.

change_note: New numbers; different error patterns (no division, sum).

title: Expected count in a 2 by 3 table
stem:
A random sample of students was classified by class year and favorite study method:
Study method: Flash cards | Notes | Videos | Row total
Freshman: 30 | 45 | 25 | 100
Sophomore: 40 | 55 | 45 | 140
Column total: 70 | 100 | 70 | table total 240
If class year and study method are independent, what is the expected count for freshmen who prefer videos?

correct.text: About 29.2
correct.rationale: Expected count = (row total x column total)/table total = (100 x 70)/240 = about 29.2.

wrong.rationale: This is the observed count for freshmen who prefer videos, not the expected count.

wrong.text: About 33.3
wrong.rationale: This is the freshman row total divided by 3 columns (100/3), which assumes equal splits across methods rather than using column totals.
wrong.error_pattern: divides row total by number of columns

wrong.rationale: This is the Videos column total divided by 2 rows (70/2), which ignores that the rows have different totals.
wrong.error_pattern: divides column total by number of rows

change_note: Gives a full table; asks for one expected cell; requires finding totals.

title: Expected count when observed is given
stem: A chi-square test of independence for 500 survey respondents focuses on one cell. The observed count in that cell is 48, its row total is 200, its column total is 150, and the table total is 500. What is the expected count for this cell?

wrong.rationale: This is the observed count in the cell, not the expected count under independence.
This adds the row and column totals (200 + 150), which is not how expected counts are computed.
This is (200/500) x (150/500), the expected proportion; it must be multiplied by 500 to get an expected count of 60.
wrong.error_pattern: gives the proportion instead of the count

change_note: Observed count distractor and proportion-vs-count error.

title: Type I error in a drug trial
stem: In a clinical trial, researchers test H0: the new drug has no effect on blood pressure. They conclude the drug lowers blood pressure, but in fact the drug has no effect. Which type of error did they make?

correct.text: Type I error, because a true null hypothesis was rejected
correct.rationale: Concluding the drug works when it truly has no effect means H0 (no effect) was true but rejected, which is a Type I error.

wrong.text: Type II error, because the drug was wrongly judged effective
wrong.rationale: Type II error is failing to reject a false null; here H0 was rejected, so it cannot be Type II.
wrong.error_pattern: swaps Type I and Type II

wrong.text: No error, because the conclusion followed from the sample results
wrong.rationale: A conclusion that follows from the data can still be wrong about the population; here H0 was true and was rejected, which is an error.
wrong.error_pattern: thinks a justified decision cannot be an error

wrong.text: Sampling bias, because the researchers used a sample
wrong.rationale: Taking a sample is not itself an error; the incorrect decision about H0 is called a Type I error.
wrong.error_pattern: confuses decision error with sampling bias

change_note: Drug trial context; different distractor set.

title: Identifying a Type II error
stem: A quality inspector tests H0: mu = 500 g for the mean fill of cereal boxes. The machine has actually drifted so that the true mean is not 500 g, but the inspector fails to reject H0. What type of error is this?

correct.text: Type II error, because a false null hypothesis was not rejected
correct.rationale: H0 (mean = 500 g) is false, and the inspector failed to reject it; that is a Type II error.

wrong.text: Type I error, because the inspector reached the wrong conclusion
wrong.rationale: Type I error is rejecting a true null; here H0 was false and was not rejected.
wrong.error_pattern: swaps Type I and Type II

wrong.text: No error, because failing to reject H0 is the safe decision
wrong.rationale: Failing to reject a false null leaves a real change undetected, which is an error even though no rejection occurred.
wrong.error_pattern: thinks not rejecting is never an error

wrong.text: Type I error, because the machine was not repaired
wrong.rationale: Whether the machine is repaired is not what defines Type I; that error requires rejecting a true H0.

change_note: Tests recognition of Type II instead of Type I; new context.

title: Probability of a Type I error
stem: A researcher tests H0 at significance level alpha = 0.05 and obtains a p-value of 0.03, so H0 is rejected. If H0 is actually true, what is the probability that this testing procedure produces a Type I error?

correct.text: 0.05, which is the significance level alpha
correct.rationale: The Type I error rate of a test is alpha; when H0 is true the procedure rejects with probability alpha = 0.05.

wrong.text: 0.03, which is the observed p-value
wrong.rationale: The p-value describes this particular sample result; the Type I error rate of the procedure is set by alpha = 0.05.
wrong.error_pattern: confuses p-value with Type I error rate

wrong.text: 0.95, which is 1 - alpha
wrong.rationale: 1 - alpha = 0.95 is the probability of not rejecting a true H0, not of rejecting it.

wrong.text: 0.97, which is 1 - the p-value
wrong.rationale: 1 - 0.03 is not a probability associated with a Type I error; the Type I error rate is alpha = 0.05.
wrong.error_pattern: uses the complement of the p-value

change_note: Asks for the Type I error rate rather than a definition; distinguishes alpha from p-value.
